name: PT Agro Bahari Nusantara Tbk

frontmatter.title: Agro Bahari Nusantara: a shrimp farmer priced for a business it has not built
frontmatter.summary: Agro Bahari farms vannamei shrimp on a pond base in Bangka Belitung. Revenue jumped once its subsidiary's ponds began harvesting, but the group still books a gross loss and a net loss, and after restating depreciation to the audited charge its EBITDA is barely positive. The share trades far above any asset or earnings benchmark we can defend. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: The operating business does not earn its cost of capital: restated to the audited depreciation charge, FY2025 EBITDA was IDR0.4bn on IDR21.6bn of sales, and EBIT stays negative through FY2029 because depreciation on the pond base exceeds the EBITDA margin [S3].

The price has detached from the assets: the shares trade on 8.4x our FY2026E book value, against a book-based value of Rp26 per share, after a documented round trip from a low tens-of-rupiah price to Rp5,200 and back [S5].

Growth from here is a pond-ramp story, not a price story. The reviewed agri deck has feed inputs rising, and a farm-gate seller cannot pass that through when imported shrimp press local prices [S8, S10].
The audited balance sheet is still liquid but is being consumed: equity fell again in FY2025 and the base case needs an external working-capital facility from FY2026 [S3, S4].

Our target of Rp22 blends a discounted cash flow worth a fraction of the asset value with the asset cross-check; it is far below the market price and we see no fundamental catalyst that closes the gap.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited accounts: the first full-year test of a positive gross margin on the completed pond base
Annual public expose: any funded expansion, capital raise or corporate action
US certification regime for Indonesian shrimp: any change to the import alert or its scope

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp22 (-90.3% from Rp224).** Agro Bahari Nusantara is a sub-scale vannamei shrimp farmer in Bangka Belitung whose shares have been priced, for most of the past year, as though a strategic buyer had already arrived rather than as a farm with a negative gross margin. our reading of the audited accounts is that the operating business is worth a fraction of its ponds and land, and that the ponds and land are worth roughly book. We have found no manipulation-class flag in the documents we hold, and the FY2025 accounts are audited [S3, S4]; it is a capital-intensive start-up at the wrong point in its cost curve, trading at a price that assumes it has already passed that point.

The variant view rests on one restatement and one observation. The restatement: the data pack carried only a fraction of the audited depreciation charge — about a fifth of the FY2024 figure and under a tenth of the FY2025 figure — while the depreciation note shows 1.2 IDR bn for FY2024 and 4.5 IDR bn for FY2025 [S3, F11, F12]. Restating flips reported EBITDA from negative to marginally positive, so the company is not bleeding at the operating line; but it also means the accounting loss is dominated by the cost of the ponds, which is the real economic cost of the business and the reason EBIT never turns positive before FY2030 in our forecast. The observation: revenue rose because the subsidiary's new ponds came into production, not because the company earns a premium price [S4, S5]. A pond-ramp story has an end date; a margin story does not.

What moves the value, in order: the farm-gate shrimp price relative to feed cost, the survival rate and feed conversion on the newly built ponds, and whether the company funds its next phase with debt, supplier credit or new shares. The first two decide whether EBIT ever crosses zero; the third decides how much of the equity the current holder keeps. Our bear case cuts growth and margin and adds G&A and capex, with a dilutive placement described in the narrative; our bull case assumes the completed ponds earn a normalised margin at a normalised price on the volume the base case already carries. The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers [S3, S4, S5].

Indonesian shrimp farming has produced several listed champions and many more small farms that never reach scale. The economics are unforgiving: a pond is a large sunk cost with a multi-year life, feed is the dominant cash cost, and survival rates can halve output in a bad cycle. Investors have historically paid for this sector on asset replacement value in the trough and on earnings at the peak, which is why a farm trading far above book with no earnings attracts attention.

UDNG is a vannamei shrimp farmer, not a poultry or feed company. Its single revenue line is the sale of raw shrimp from its own ponds; there is no feed mill, no hatchery, no processing plant and no branded consumer product in the audited accounts [S3]. It sits in our poultry and protein coverage because that is where the industry map places shrimp aquaculture, but readers should treat every poultry-feed benchmark with care: the company buys feed, it does not make it.

The operating footprint is two sites in Bangka Belitung. At Dusun Sika in West Bangka the company runs 14.0 ponds production ponds (ten intensive and four super-intensive) on 41,966 m2 of pond area, supported by three reservoir ponds and four wastewater treatment ponds [S4, F26, F28]. At Tanjung Kemirai in South Bangka its wholly owned subsidiary PT Marina Bahari Sentosa finished construction of 34.0 ponds ponds, with commissioning starting in February 2025 [S4, F27]. The company injected roughly forty billion rupiah of IPO proceeds into that subsidiary in December 2023 to build the new site [S5]. Management describes the model as technology-based, data-driven cultivation with biosecurity and water-quality control, and its stated priorities are survival rate, feed conversion and market diversification [S5].

The commercial structure is thin and concentrated. The group employed 15.0 people permanent staff at the end of FY2025, a headcount that is small relative to the pond count and implies most pond labour is contracted or casual [S4, F29]. Sales go to a handful of domestic buyers: PT Wirontono Baru took 12.8 IDR bn of FY2025 revenue and PT Anesta Agung was the second customer above the disclosure threshold, with all sales made to third parties [S3, F37]. There is no disclosed export customer, export certification or offtake contract, which matters because the farm-gate price it receives is set by traders and processors downstream of it rather than by the end market [S3, S5].

Ownership is founder-controlled but not a conglomerate structure. Vincent Lukito and Jose Loupiga Keliat each hold about a fifth of the shares, Christian Brandon Limbono holds a smaller stake, and the public holds the rest; the president director is also one of the two largest shareholders [S5]. Equity of 51.8 sits against an accumulated deficit of -7.0 IDR bn, the residue of losses since the subsidiary began spending [S3, F38]. The company listed in October 2023 and has not raised equity since [S5].

Shrimp grow-out is a licence-to-operate business more than a brand business. The physical asset is a pond with pumps, aerators and a water-treatment system; the know-how is in stocking density, feed management and disease control; and the output is a commodity priced by size grade. That is why listed shrimp farmers in the region are valued on replacement cost when they lose money and on earnings only when survival rates and prices are both favourable.

Indonesia is a large aquaculture producer and shrimp is its highest-value export line. National aquaculture output reached 5.0 m tonnes in FY2025, close to the government's target, and shrimp exports were worth 1.4 USD bn with double-digit growth, according to the industry data reproduced in the company's annual report [S4, F33, F35]. Productivity on intensive ponds has risen to 19.1 t/ha, which is the benchmark against which a farm of this size should be measured [S4, F34]. The demand side is genuinely global; the supply side is fragmented, cyclical and exposed to disease and weather, which is why prices swing far more than volumes.

The trade regime is the dominant external variable. The United States applies a tariff of 19.0% on Indonesian shrimp [S4, F32]. Separately, the US Food and Drug Administration imposed an import alert in late 2025 after radioactive caesium was detected in frozen shrimp and cloves; the Indonesian task force states the restriction applies to product from Java and Lampung, that certification rather than a ban is required, and that the contamination was traced to a metal-processing source in Cikande rather than to farms or cultivation practice [S9]. Bangka Belitung, where UDNG farms, is outside the restricted origin list, which is a relative advantage, but the price effect of the alert is national because buyers discount the origin as a whole [S4, S9].

Domestic policy has moved against the farmer. The government imported 219 tonnes of shrimp from Argentina and Ecuador in May and June 2026, and farmer representatives say the inflow depressed farm-gate prices just as local harvests peaked [S10, F36]. The fisheries minister has acknowledged that prices fell in several regions even as the rupiah weakened, and attributes the weakness to a domestic hatchery sector that is not adequate and to feed raw materials that are still entirely imported [S8]. For a farm that sells domestically and buys imported feed, that combination is the worst of both worlds: costs are set abroad and prices are set at home.

Our reviewed agri deck has the feed complex rising from its FY2025 base into FY2026 and FY2027 before flattening, with soymeal, wheat and corn all above last year's average. Because the rupiah is the reporting currency and feed is imported, a weaker rupiah amplifies the move. We carry that through a single soymeal cost link rather than a basket, since soymeal is the main traded protein input in a vannamei formulation and corn is not a material shrimp-feed ingredient [S3, S8].

Competitive position: UDNG is a challenger with no structural moat. It has no brand, no switching costs, no proprietary genetics, no feed integration, no processing margin and no distribution density; its assets are pond sites, biosecurity know-how and a licence to operate. The five forces are uniformly unfavourable. Buyer power is high and visible in the customer concentration [S3]. Supplier power is high because feed is imported and the hatchery sector is weak [S8]. Rivalry is high because output is a commodity and the government is willing to import to stabilise consumer prices [S10]. Entry barriers are moderate, since ponds can be built wherever coastal permits allow. Substitutes exist at the consumer level in other proteins. What the company controls is cost per kilogram and survival rate, and those are operational rather than structural advantages a competitor cannot copy.

Shrimp aquaculture is one of the few Indonesian protein industries where the country holds a genuine global cost advantage, but the advantage accrues mostly to integrated exporters with their own hatcheries, feed relationships and cold chain. Standalone grow-out farms typically capture the most volatile slice of the value chain: they bear disease and price risk while the processor and the importer capture the branded margin.

Revenue history is a three-year cycle, not a trend. FY2023, the last full year on the original fourteen ponds, earned 8.3 of sales and 2.6 of gross profit, a 30.6% margin, with operating profit of 0.2 [S11]. FY2024 collapsed to 3.1 and a gross margin of -66.9%, a year before the caesium finding [S3]. FY2025's 21.6 was the subsidiary's ponds entering harvest rather than a price gain, and cost of sales rose faster than sales to 22.6, so the group booked a gross loss of -1.0 [S3]. General and administrative expense of 3.1 took the operating loss to -4.0 and the net loss to -3.4 [S3]. Our forecast has revenue compounding from 28.1 in FY2026 to 46.9 in FY2030 as the built pond base is fully utilised, and the gross margin swinging from -4.7% to 9.8% [S3, S4, S5].

The revenue path is a pond-utilisation path, not a price path, and that is the weakest link in the evidence. The company discloses 14.0 ponds ponds on 41,966 m2 at the original site and 34.0 ponds new ponds at the subsidiary, but not the new site's area; the only productivity benchmark in the filings is 19.1 t/ha on intensive ponds [S4]. FY2023's revenue per pond, spread over the enlarged footprint, lands close to our FY2026 revenue, which is why we treat FY2026 as the first full-year run-rate rather than growth. The step from FY2026 to FY2030 requires revenue per pond to rise by more than half again, from survival-rate and feed-conversion gains and a normalisation of farm-gate prices. We cannot test that against tonnes per hectare because neither tonnage sold nor the new site's area is disclosed; that is a gap in the evidence, and it is why the DCF rather than the growth path carries the valuation.

The cost structure is the story. Feed is 10.6 IDR bn in FY2025, the largest single line of cost of sales, and it is bought, not milled [S3, F25]. Depreciation is 4.5, close to a fifth of sales, and it is the charge that decides the equity value: it is fixed on a pond base that has already been built, so a larger harvest dilutes it per kilogram [S3]. We forecast D&A falling from 17.0% of revenue in FY2026 to 10.0% in FY2030, and the D&A-to-revenue ratio, not the EBITDA margin, is why EBIT stays negative through FY2029. EBITDA is -0.2 in FY2026 rising to 6.0 in FY2030, while EBIT moves from -5.0 to 1.3 over the same span [S3].

Cash generation is the weak link. FY2025 delivered operating cash flow of 0.2 IDR bn against capex of 5.2, so free cash flow was negative and the difference came out of a cash balance that fell from 8.2 to 2.7 [S3]. We do not credit a working-capital release: the June 2026 vendor snapshot shows negative working capital, but no half-year report is archived to support it, so we hold operating working capital at the audited absolute balance of 2.6 through the forecast [S2, S3]. On those inputs free cash flow is still negative in FY2027 at -2.1, turns positive in FY2028 at 0.1 and peaks in FY2030 at 2.0, so the group needs outside funding through the middle of the period.

The balance sheet is levered only by leases, with debt of 0.6 and cash of 2.7 at the audited FY2025 year end, so net debt is -2.1 and the group carried no bank facility [S3]. Equity fell from 55.2 to 51.8 on the year's loss [S3]. We value off this audited balance sheet, not the unaudited June 2026 vendor snapshot, because no half-year report is archived [S2, S3]. There is 10.5 IDR bn of land advances on the balance sheet for purchases in Tempilang and Tukak Sadai where the title upgrade is still in process; we treat these as real assets but do not add them to the operating forecast, since no development plan or permit timeline is disclosed [S4, F31].

The base case is funded explicitly. A working-capital facility is drawn at IDR0.8bn in FY2026, then again in FY2027, FY2028 and FY2029; debt peaks at 6.1 and interest is charged at the lease-like cost of debt. From FY2030, once the built ponds throw off free cash flow, the facility is amortised, and debt falls to 0.4 by FY2035 while cash builds to 7.0. Every year keeps cash positive, with the low point at 0.1 in FY2027, which is why the FY2027 draw is the largest of the four. That is a financing assumption sized only to keep the balance sheet solvent while the ponds ramp, not a growth enabler; a dilutive equity raise remains the alternative and sits in the bear case [S3, S4].

Capital allocation has been a single decision repeated: raise equity at listing, spend it on ponds, and fund the gap since with supplier credit, cash and now a working-capital facility [S5, S3]. No dividend has been paid or declared since the October 2023 listing, and payout is forecast at zero [S3, S5]. The risk is that the next phase is funded by new shares rather than internal cash, which is why dilution is in the bear case rather than the base.

Earnings-quality flags, per the house screen. Accruals: net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets is positive in FY2023, close to zero in FY2024 and negative in FY2025, when a net loss of -3.4 sat against operating cash flow of 0.2 IDR bn on a smaller asset base — cash ahead of earnings, the opposite of the usual red flag [S3, F15, F47]. Receivables are not growing faster than revenue: trade receivables are one customer and about a month of sales [S3]. The pressure is on the cost side, where depreciation was understated in the data pack and has been restated [S3, F11, F12]. No special-monitoring-board status or special notation letter is disclosed, and no pledge of the controlling stakes is disclosed [S4, S3]; on the audit we make no claim, because the archived filing text does not include the signed auditor's report page. The IDX regime flag that does apply is two cooling-down suspensions in 2026, the first after a sharp cumulative fall and the second after a cumulative rise, a market-conduct issue rather than an accounting one [S6, S7]. Related-party revenue and receivables are nil: the related-party note discloses no sales or balances with related parties, and the largest customer is a third party [S3]. Classification: optics-class on disclosure and cost allocation, no manipulation-class flag found on the evidence available.

For a pond-based farm, the accounting loss and the economic loss can diverge for years. During a build-out the depreciation charge runs ahead of the harvest it supports, so a company can be cash-generative at the EBITDA line and loss-making at the net line. The test that matters is whether the fully built asset eventually earns more than its cost of capital, not whether a single year's net income is positive.

We value a shrimp grow-out farm on the cash its ponds generate and on what those ponds would cost to replace, and we give no weight to earnings multiples. That is not a stylistic preference: with EBIT negative through FY2029 the shares trade on 891.0x last year's EBITDA and a price-to-earnings ratio that cannot be computed, so the industry default mix of discounted cash flow, P/E and EV/EBITDA collapses into a single usable method [S0, S3]. We deliberately run two methods rather than the house convention of a primary plus two cross-checks: for a farm whose revenue is a commodity price times a fixed output, a sales multiple and an earnings multiple are both contaminated by the same price variable, so adding a third would add arithmetic rather than information. We weight the discounted cash flow at 50% and a price-to-book (P/BV) cross-check at 50%. The P/B is the only cross-check we can source for a listed Indonesian shrimp grow-out farm because there is no pure shrimp comparable; the peer table below shows what we used and its limits.

The cost of capital is built from a government bond yield of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country premium of 2.5% and an unlevered beta of 0.90 taken low because the listed agri comparables are mostly diversified processors rather than pure farms. The bond yield is net of the Indonesia sovereign default spread of 1.62% embedded in the deck's risk-free series, and that term is subtracted rather than added: capitalising the country premium inside the equity risk premium without the deduction would double-count Indonesia's default risk and overstate the hurdle. Leverage is negligible — the group carries leases only, with debt of 0.6 against equity of 51.8 [S3] — so the levered beta is 0.90 and the cost of equity is 11.9%. Lease interest in the filing implies a single-digit cost (F23 on F21), while the engine prices debt off the sovereign plus a corporate spread; at a debt weight of 0.2% the difference moves WACC by only a few basis points, so the resulting WACC of 11.9% is within a few basis points of the cost of equity [S3, S0]. That is the right answer for an all-equity-financed company, and it means the discount rate is not doing hidden work in our valuation.

On the primary method, free cash flow to the firm is -3.0 in FY2026 and -2.1 in FY2027, turns positive at 0.1 in FY2028 and peaks at 2.0 in FY2030, then settles just below that level as capex is held at the depreciation charge and the ponds stop needing to grow. Discounted at 11.9% with terminal growth of 4.0%, that gives an enterprise value of 9.8 and an equity value of Rp7 a share, and the terminal value is 71.8% of the enterprise value. That is a high dependence and it is the method's real weakness here: the explicit years are thin — free cash flow only clears zero in FY2028 — so most of the 9.8 is the perpetuity. Because the DCF then adds the net cash on the balance sheet, the terminal value is a somewhat lower share of the equity than of the enterprise value, but the point stands: strip the perpetuity and the ponds are worth only a little more than the net cash the company already holds [S3, S4]. The terminal-value test is passed, not waived. The terminal year carries EBIT of 1.9 on EBITDA of 7.3, so the implied exit multiple on the perpetuity is under three times terminal EBITDA and about ten times that EBIT — against an entry of 891.0x last year's EBITDA. The DCF therefore assumes the multiple collapses from today's price to something a rational buyer would pay for a mature farm and still finds a value, however small; nothing in the answer depends on multiple expansion [S0, S3]. There is also no reinvestment engine to model: capex is held at the depreciation charge once the ponds are built, so growth is not manufactured by compounding retained capital at a high incremental return — the value rests entirely on the return the existing ponds earn, and that return sits below the cost of capital in every year of the forecast.

FY2023 is the counter-example the bull case rightly points to. On the original pond base the group earned 30.6% gross and 0.2 of operating profit [S11]. It cannot simply return: the 34.0 ponds new ponds carry the depreciation that took the group charge to 4.5 [S3, F11, F12], and revenue per pond has fallen since FY2023 as farm-gate prices and the caesium discount hit the same footprint [S3, S4]. A return to the FY2023 gross margin at today's revenue would be a bull case well beyond the three-point margin improvement we carry, and even that bull case values the shares far below the current price.

The cross-check values the same assets at book. Tangible book is 29.6 per share at FY2025 [S3], and we apply 0.9 times a blended animal-protein book benchmark to reach Rp26, which is 291.3% above the discounted cash flow. The peer table is below, and the cohort behind that multiple has to be read with it: the engine's median runs across ten animal-protein names, two of which are extreme in opposite directions — one trades at a fraction of book, one at a high single-digit multiple — and the median it prints is 0.9. The five core poultry names, CPIN, JPFA, CPRO, SIPD and WMPP, sit at a median close to one times book, and dropping the two extremes leaves a median a little above one; either would lift the book leg by a few rupiah a share and the twelve-month target by less than that, so we show the engine's number and disclose what sits behind it. We could not find a listed shrimp grow-out comparable in Indonesia: the closest names are poultry and animal-protein processors whose returns, leverage and cycle differ from a single-site farmer, so the peer-median multiple is a cross-check on asset value, not an earnings multiple. The reader can see the weight from two points: at half book the book leg halves, and at one-and-a-half times book it rises by half again; a shrimp-specific multiple does not exist, and we do not invent one. The divergence is the whole argument of this note, so we state both sides. The DCF is right if the ponds keep earning a margin below their depreciation charge, in which case replacement cost is not a floor, it is a ceiling on what a rational buyer pays. The book value is right if a strategic or state-linked buyer wants the coastal sites and the licences and will pay carrying value for them regardless of the earnings stream — the shrimp sector has seen exactly that kind of consolidation interest, and the land advances for Tempilang and Tukak Sadai show management expects to expand the footprint [S4, F31]. Book includes 10.5 IDR bn of land advances whose title is still in process; at a discount multiple those are credited at about nine-tenths of face, and a buyer who will not pay for unperfected title would cut the book leg by roughly a fifth. We are not aware of any bid, letter of intent or disclosed negotiation, so the asset value is a backstop rather than a forecast [S5, S6].

The sensitivity table is a slope on the upside and a floor on the downside. A two-percentage-point change in the gross margin moves the twelve-month value by a couple of rupiah in either direction, and a four-point change in annual revenue growth moves it by rather less, because the operating business is the smaller part of the blended value; the WACC and terminal-growth grid moves the DCF leg by a few rupiah, which the blend halves. The asymmetry matters: as the margin is cut, the DCF leg falls toward zero and the engine floors it there, so the bottom rows of the table converge on the bear value and barely move, while the top rows keep adding. That is the honest picture — with the operating business worth well under the book value, the answer is governed by the asset leg, and the table shows how little of it the cash flow can take away [S3, S4].

What the price implies. At Rp224 the shares are on 8.4x our FY2026E book value and 891.0x last year's EBITDA — FY2026E EBITDA is negative at the deck's feed price, so that multiple cannot be computed — on a market capitalisation of IDR392.0bn against a free float of 49.0% [S0]. To justify that on assets alone, a buyer would have to believe the ponds and land are worth several times their carrying value; to justify it on earnings, the company would have to reach a margin it has never reported. Neither case is supported by anything we can source. What the record does support is that the price has travelled from a low tens-of-rupiah level to Rp5,200 and back to Rp224 inside a year, with two trading suspensions for abnormal price movement along the way [S5, S6, S7]. We think that history, not a fundamental re-rating, explains the current multiple.

Blending 50% of the discounted cash flow with 50% of the book cross-check gives an intrinsic value of Rp17 per share; after rolling forward a year at the cost of equity and deducting the dividend we expect over the next twelve months (Rp0), the twelve-month target is Rp22, a total return of -90.3% from Rp224 [S0, S3]. We rate the shares SELL. The book leg is the larger share of that value — the discounted cash flow supplies the rest at Rp7 against Rp26 — and we weight P/B at 50.0%, cut from the earlier draft, so the reader can see the effect at half and one-and-a-half times book above. The engine rolls the blended value forward at the cost of equity, which adds Rp19 less Rp17; on a book that is falling (29.6 to 26.7), the correct roll on the asset leg is negative, so the target is, if anything, overstated. We have not overridden the engine convention; the direction of the call does not depend on it.

Asset-backed commodity producers are usually valued in a band between replacement cost and the present value of mid-cycle cash flow. The band collapses toward replacement cost when the asset is losing money and toward cash flow when it is earning; a price above the top of the band is normally paid only for control, for a turnaround with a named catalyst, or for scarcity of float. When none of those is present, the premium tends to decay as liquidity returns.

The risks that matter are concentrated in three places: the trade regime, the domestic price policy and the funding of a company that does not yet cover its capex from operations. We rank each by likelihood and by the size of the hit to our value.

Trade and certification, high likelihood, high impact. The United States applies a tariff of 19.0% to Indonesian shrimp and, since late 2025, a certification regime following the caesium detection, which the government says is not a total ban and which is traced to a processing source rather than to farms [S4, S9]. Even though Bangka Belitung is outside the restricted list, national origin discounts hit every seller, and the company's own annual report names the contamination finding as a cause of the FY2025 gross loss [S4]. A widening of the alert or a retaliatory step would remove the export option the company needs to escape domestic prices.

Domestic price policy, high likelihood, high impact. The government imported 219 tonnes of shrimp in the middle of the 2026 harvest and farmers reported falling farm-gate prices as a result [S10]. The fisheries ministry attributes the weakness to an inadequate hatchery sector and fully imported feed raw materials [S8]. A government that prioritises cheap protein for consumers over farm-gate margins can repeat the intervention at will, and this company has no contractual protection against it.

Input cost and currency, high likelihood, medium impact. Feed is the largest cost line at 10.6 IDR bn and its raw materials are imported [S3, S8], so a weaker rupiah and a rising soymeal deck both compress a margin that does not yet cover the depreciation charge. We model the deck through a single soymeal link, which means an adverse move is captured on the cost side but only partly offset by price.

Operational, medium likelihood, high impact. A single province, a small number of ponds and a biological product with no insurance against disease mean one bad cycle can halve output. Survival rate and feed conversion are the only levers management names, and neither is contractually visible to an outside holder [S5].

Funding and liquidity, medium likelihood, high impact. Operating cash flow of 0.2 IDR bn did not cover capex of 5.2 in FY2025, and the base case needs a working-capital facility from FY2026 to FY2029 to keep cash positive; we carry that facility and charge interest on it. We do not credit the negative working capital in the June 2026 vendor snapshot, because no half-year report is archived [S2, S3]. A rights issue at the current price would be deeply dilutive for anyone buying today, which is why dilution sits in the bear case rather than the base.

Governance and conduct, medium likelihood, medium impact. Control sits with the founders and the public float is 49.0% [S5, S0]. The shares were suspended twice in 2026: the first in March after a sharp cumulative fall, the second in September after a cumulative rise, both under the exchange's cooling-down rule [S6, S7]. Nothing in the documents we hold evidences misuse, but a controlled company with a history of suspension and a price that has moved by multiples is not a place to assume orderly exit.

The float is not thin. At 49.0% free float and daily turnover of about one percent of the market capitalisation, the premium is not a scarcity-of-paper story [S0]. The company attributes the 2026 sell-off to an MSCI index rebalancing combined with Middle East geopolitics [S5]; an index deletion is the one identifiable forced-selling mechanism here, and we treat MSCI status, not float, as the convergence trigger.

The bear case carries probability 30.0% and a twelve-month value of Rp15; the base case 50.0% at Rp19; the bull case 20.0% at Rp40. Weighting those three gives Rp22, which is the target Rp22 (no liquidity discount). The bear is anchored on FY2024, when revenue fell -62.5% — from 8.3 to 3.1 — and the gross margin turned to -66.9% a year before the caesium finding [S3]; even so we use a much milder version than that collapse — a ten-percentage-point growth cut, a three-point margin cut, two points more G&A and one point more capex — mirrored in the bull. Three things about the weighting have to be said plainly. First, the bear is flat rather than loose: its operating cuts drive the discounted-cash-flow leg toward zero, where the engine floors it, so the bear value is essentially the book leg alone and the shocks cannot take it much lower. Second, the bull is convex for the same reason in reverse — it is the only state in which the ponds earn a real return — so on a fifth probability it supplies about a third of the Rp22 blend, and the bull's upside is not a claim that a happy outcome is likely. Third, the bull adds margin and capex recovery, not volume: the revenue ramp sits in the base case already, which is the disclosed optimism in this model, so the asymmetry is in the arithmetic of a floored DCF, not in the shock sizes, which are mirrored. The bear narrative also carries a dilutive placement: the base cash flow does not cover capex and the facility is a bridge, so new shares are the likely route if the harvest disappoints. The engine does not apply a change in share count to per-share value, so the bear number is an upper bound on the dilution case; at a placement of a fifth of the register the current holder's share of the equity would fall by a sixth.

What would change our view, in order of importance: an audited FY2026 gross margin above the depreciation charge, which would make the DCF the wrong method and justify book value or better [S3]; a settled US certification regime with no origin discount [S9]; a disclosed and funded expansion that converts the land advances into productive ponds [S4, F31]; and evidence of a strategic buyer for the sites, which is the only fundamental route to the market price [S5].

Small-cap commodity producers commonly trade far above fundamental value for a period after a listing, because the float is small, the story is simple and the sellers are few. The premium usually closes when the free float widens, when a placement is priced, or when a period of illiquidity reminds holders that the exit is narrow. None of those events needs to be dramatic; a sequence of ordinary disclosure dates is usually enough.

Ownership and control. The company is founder-controlled and has no corporate parent. Vincent Lukito and Jose Loupiga Keliat each hold a stake of roughly a fifth, Christian Brandon Limbono holds a smaller block, and the public holds the remainder; insiders are recorded at 51.0% of the register with 49.0% free float [S5, S0]. The president director is one of the two largest shareholders, so management and control are the same people and minority holders have no independent lever beyond the annual meeting [S5]. There is no evidence of a conglomerate structure, cross-holdings or a family vehicle behind the listed entity.

Related parties and structure flags. Sales are made to third parties and the two customers above the disclosure threshold, PT Wirontono Baru and PT Anesta Agung, are not described as related parties [S3, F37]. We found no disclosed related-party revenue, no loans to affiliates and no guarantees to shareholder ventures in the documents we hold [S3, S4]. No pledge or encumbrance of the controlling stakes is disclosed [S4], and the company has not undertaken a rights issue, a private placement at a discount or a fixed-asset revaluation that would inflate book value since listing [S3, S5]. The structure flags that do apply are the ones from the earnings-quality screen: a part-year harvest loaded with a full depreciation charge, a thin permanent headcount with most pond labour contracted, and a land purchase where the title upgrade is still in process [S3, S4, F31].

Auditor and accounts. Our history is taken from the audited FY2025 consolidated accounts and restated where the data pack disagrees, most importantly depreciation [S3, F11, F12]. The archived text of that filing does not include the signed independent auditor's report page, so we make no claim about the opinion itself and flag it as an open item: an unmodified opinion would be expected, a qualification or a going-concern paragraph would change our view of the downside.

Dividend record and capital allocation. No dividend has been paid or declared since the October 2023 listing, and the company carries an accumulated deficit of -7.0 IDR bn [S3, F38]. Payout is forecast at zero through the horizon because the cash is needed for maintenance capex and working capital [S3, S5]. Capital allocation is therefore a single question for holders: whether the retained cash and any new funding earn more than the cost of capital, which the FY2025 margin says they do not.

ESG exposures. The company publishes a sustainability report inside its annual report and its disclosed priorities are water quality, biosecurity and community programmes around the pond sites [S4]. The material exposures for a shrimp farm are effluent and mangrove conversion at the coastal sites, antibiotic and chemical use that buyers test for, and contracted labour on the ponds that sits outside the permanent headcount of 15.0 people [S4, F29]. The caesium episode is an industry-level reputational exposure this company inherits without having caused it, and it is the clearest example of an ESG factor that has already cost shareholders money [S4, S9]. Governance on disclosure is adequate for a company of this size: quarterly statements, an annual report, a public expose and a shareholding register are all published [S3, S4, S5].

Indonesian small caps with founder control and a free float below half are a familiar governance profile: the controller sets strategy, the independent commissioners are few, and minority holders rely on disclosure rather than on voting. The practical test is not the formal structure but whether related-party flows are disclosed and priced, and whether the controller funds the company with equity at fair value rather than with debt or discounted paper.

Dated events that can move the shares. The FY2026 audited accounts, expected by the end of March 2027, are the first full-year test of whether the completed pond base produces a gross margin above the depreciation charge; that single number decides whether the discounted cash flow or the book cross-check deserves the higher weight [S3, S4]. The annual public expose, normally held in June, is where any funded expansion, capital raise or corporate action would be disclosed first; the 2026 expose on 17 June targeted 2026 as an acceleration year through higher sales volume, cost efficiency and asset optimisation, but gave no numeric revenue or margin target [S5]. The US certification regime around Indonesian shrimp is dated by the alert itself and by any change in scope, and is the fastest-moving external variable for the farm-gate price [S9].

Between those dates we monitor a short list of operational numbers rather than the share price. Revenue and gross margin per quarter, against the run-rate needed to turn EBIT positive [S3]. Pond productivity in tonnes per hectare, against the national intensive benchmark of 19.1 t/ha, and any disclosed survival rate or feed conversion ratio [S4, F34]. Average selling price per kilogram against the feed cost per kilogram, which is the margin driver we can actually observe [S3, F25]. Cash and payables at each audited year end and in any archived half-year report, because the harvest cycle is funded by supplier credit and a working-capital facility [S3]. Any new share issuance, pledge or related-party transaction, which would move the governance assessment [S5]. Government import volumes and any change to the origin certification list, which set the domestic price [S9, S10]. MSCI index status and any deletion or rebalancing, which the company names as the forced-selling mechanism behind the 2026 drawdown [S5].

We will also track the two market-conduct items: whether the trading suspensions are lifted and on what conditions, and whether the free float widens through a placement or a sell-down by the founders [S6, S7, S5]. A widening float would probably compress the premium; a placement at a discount would confirm the funding risk in the bear case.

For a commodity producer the monitoring list is short and physical: cost per unit, output per unit of capacity, and the price the market pays. Everything else — the narrative, the index membership, the short-term price — follows those three with a lag. A holder who tracks them quarterly usually sees a change in the fundamental case before it reaches the disclosure calendar.

bear.narrative: A repeat of the FY2024 harvest failure in milder form: revenue growth is cut, the gross margin absorbs a price and survival-rate shock, fixed G&A is spread over less output and maintenance capex overruns. FY2024 showed revenue falling 62% and the gross margin turning to -66.7% a year before the Cesium-137 finding [S3], so a biological or price shock is a live precedent. The shocks are deliberately modest relative to that precedent: a 10pp revenue-growth cut, a 3pp margin cut, 2pp more G&A and 1pp more capex, mirrored in the bull case. A dilutive placement is also carried in this case: the base cash flow does not cover capex and no bank facility is disclosed [S3], so new shares are the likely funding route if the harvest disappoints.

bull.narrative: The built-out Marina Bahari Sentosa ponds run at full survival rate and better FCR, farm-gate prices normalise once the Cesium-137 certification issue is settled, G&A is spread over a much larger harvest and maintenance capex comes in below plan, lifting the margin faster than the feed deck rises. No share issuance is needed in this case, so the count stays at today's register.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025's +590% was a base effect, not a run-rate: subsidiary PT Marina Bahari Sentosa began commercial harvest only in 2025 after completing 34 ponds from February 2025, alongside 14 company ponds [S4]. FY2026-27 growth is the full-year run-rate of those already-built ponds plus survival-rate/FCR gains the public expose targets [S5], tempered by weak farm-gate shrimp prices and 219t of imported shrimp competing with local harvests in mid-2026 [S8, S10]. Growth then fades toward nominal GDP as the built-out pond base is fully utilised; no new pond capacity is assumed because no funded expansion plan is disclosed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025's -4.5% gross margin [S3] is not the steady state: the annual report attributes the gross loss to the Cesium-137 contamination finding on Indonesian frozen shrimp, which depressed selling prices and harvest absorption [S4], and to fixed pond depreciation loaded onto a part-year harvest. FY2023, the last year the original pond base ran without the expansion, earned a 30.6% audited gross margin [S11], so the model can earn a margin once the fixed deposit is spread over a full harvest. FY2026 is calibrated so that at FY2025 soymeal prices the group reproduces FY2025's 2.02% EBITDA margin (the -2% line plus 13% G&A minus 17% D&A); the model's reported FY2026 margin is lower only because the reviewed soymeal deck stands above its FY2025 average, and that feed drag is carried by the link below, not double-counted here. The path then recovers as the fixed D&A and G&A base is absorbed by the built-out ponds, reaching a post-D&A margin consistent with a fully utilised 48-pond footprint: 14 company ponds at Dusun Sika plus 34 at the subsidiary [S4], against the approximately 45 ponds management cites in the public expose [S5]. The last years of the path also carry the long-run recovery of feed cost that the link's within-year pass-through deliberately withholds: the reviewed deck's long-run soymeal price sits about 40% above FY2025's average, of which the evidence says only a fifth is recovered in the farm-gate price within the year [S8, S10], but a permanent 40% cost level would also lift the shrimp price the farmer sells into over a full cycle, because feed is the industry's dominant cost and sets its supply curve. The within-year stickiness is therefore charged in FY2026-29 and released in the terminal state, so the steady state earns the roughly 10% post-depreciation margin a fully utilised farm should earn rather than a permanently loss-making one.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Feed is 47% of cost of sales [S3 note 21]; soymeal is roughly a quarter of a vannamei feed formulation (below the poultry share, because shrimp feed leans on fishmeal and wheat gluten too), so 47% x 25% puts the soymeal-exposed share of total COGS at about 12%. The link scales COGS only by the deck's move away from the FY2025 base, so the 12% is an exposure weight, not a forecast of feed cost.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: A small pond farmer is a price taker: the fisheries minister says feed raw materials are fully imported and farm-gate shrimp prices fell in several regions even as the dollar strengthened [S8], and imported shrimp volume in mid-2026 depressed the price just as local harvests peaked [S10]. Only about a fifth of a feed-cost move is therefore recoverable in the offtake price within the year, so the pass-through is set at 20% and the remaining four-fifths compresses the margin. The parameter and this basis agree; the DCF is a small part of the blend, so the effect is on the FY2026 line, not on the target.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 G&A was Rp3.06bn, 14.2% of a part-year revenue base, with only 15 permanent employees [S3, S4]; listed-company and audit costs are largely fixed, so the ratio falls as harvest revenue scales. At the forecast revenue base the fixed Rp3.1bn cost is about 5-6% of sales, so the long-run anchor is 6.5% rather than a 9% floor that would double-count growth in the cost base.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation is restated from the LK to Rp4.48bn in FY2025 (the data pack carried a fraction of it) [S3 note 12]. The charge is close to fixed on the Rp44bn pond base, so it falls from ~21% of sales in FY2025 as the same assets harvest more revenue, to about 9% of sales at full utilisation; the terminal charge and terminal capex are set equal, so the asset base is held constant in perpetuity.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex of Rp5.2bn (24% of sales) and FY2024's Rp8.5bn were the build-out of the 34 Marina Bahari Sentosa ponds, completed in 2025 [S3, S4]. With no funded new capacity disclosed, forward capex is pond maintenance and equipment replacement. It steps down while the new ponds are still in their early harvest years, then rises back to equal the terminal D&A charge: a steady-state terminal year with capex at 9% of sales and D&A at 9% holds the pond base constant, so the Gordon terminal value is not fed by an asset base that is being run down [S3, S4]. The Rp10.5bn land advances already paid are sunk and sit on the balance sheet, not in forecast capex.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital is held at its audited FY2025 absolute level of about Rp2.58bn [S3], expressed as a falling share of revenue because the standing shrimp stock is tied to the fixed pond base, not to sales: the bulk of it is biological assets of Rp4.16bn net of trade payables of Rp2.84bn [S3], a stock that does not grow proportionally once the 48 ponds are built and stocked. No archived half-year report supports the negative working capital in the June 2026 vendor snapshot, so the forecast neither releases cash nor assumes unlimited supplier credit; the ratio declines only because revenue grows over a constant working-capital stock.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 booked only a deferred tax benefit of Rp621m on a Rp4.05bn pre-tax loss [S3]; forecast loss years carry no tax credit (no further deferred tax asset is credited on losses), and the 22% statutory rate applies once accumulated losses are used up.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The only borrowings are lease liabilities bearing Rp49m of interest on a Rp0.62bn balance in FY2025 [S3, note 11], i.e. about 8%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: The LK reports no interest income line and cash sits in transaction accounts [S3], so a 2% deposit yield is assumed on the average operating balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No bank facility is disclosed beyond leases at FY2025 [S3], but the base case cannot fund its harvest ramp from operating cash: capex plus working capital exceed EBITDA until FY2029. We therefore carry an explicit working-capital facility, drawn only as needed to keep the cash balance non-negative: Rp0.8bn in FY2026, Rp1.8bn in FY2027, Rp1.6bn in FY2028 and Rp1.3bn in FY2029, peaking at Rp5.5bn. From FY2030, once the built ponds throw off free cash flow, the facility is amortised at Rp0.9bn a year and is repaid to a small stub by FY2035; that is the falling debt line the engine prints and the one Section 3 describes, and every year of the schedule keeps cash positive. It is a financing assumption, not a growth enabler, and it is priced at the lease-like cost of debt already in the model. A dilutive equity raise remains a live alternative and is carried in the bear case.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating income is disclosed beyond a Rp44m FY2025 residual [S3]; set to zero.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interest is Rp1,000 in a single 99.99% subsidiary, PT Marina Bahari Sentosa [S3], so the minority share of profit is negligible.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid or declared since the 2023 IPO and the company is in accumulated deficit of Rp7.0bn [S3, S5]; payout is set to zero across the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Base case holds 1,750,040,072 shares [S5]; no rights issue or private placement has been announced. A capital raise is a live risk given the cash burn and is carried in the bear case narrative, not the base.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR cash flows (4%), below long-run Indonesian nominal GDP and consistent with a domestic shrimp producer whose output is constrained by pond area and coastal permits. It is applied to a terminal year in which capex equals D&A and the EBIT margin is stable, so the Gordon value is not a plug for a shrinking asset base.

challenges.challenge: The named variant view is misstated. The summary says the data pack carries depreciation of 1.2 in FY2024 and 4.5 in FY2025 while the notes show 4.5 and 1.2 — the reverse of the register: restated[] shows pack 0.229 (FY2024) and 0.342 (FY2025) against filing 1.180 (F12) and 4.485 (F11). challenges.challenge: 60% of the weight and 94% of the value (Rp24.65 of a Rp15.60 v0) comes from P/B at a 0.895x median taken from a poultry-feed peer set the report own section 1 says is not comparable (CPIN 1.11x, JPFA 0.81x, CPRO 0.47x, SIPD 0.98x, WMPP 1.51x, AYAM 9.15x, NEST 0.005x). No shrimp grow-out comparable is used or discussed and the peer table is not shown.
challenges.answer: Cut the P/B weight from 60% to 50%, added {{table:peers}} with the animal-protein names, and stated plainly that no listed shrimp grow-out comp exists, so the peer-median P/B is an asset cross-check rather than a shrimp earnings multiple. Also gave the half-book and one-and-a-half-times-book values in words and flagged the land-advance haircut. The DCF is Rp1.6/share, so the asset leg dominates by construction, not by weight alone. [S0, S3]

challenges.challenge: The DCF terminal year is not a steady state: FCFF declines every year FY2030-FY2035 (0.69, 0.32, 0.27, 0.21, 0.14, 0.07) while the Gordon terminal assumes +4% forever; EBIT deteriorates to -3.12 and D&A rises to 5.98 against capex of 3.59, so the positive FCFF exists only through a capex-below-depreciation gap that shrinks the asset base. Terminal value is -19.8% of EV and EV (-1.7) sits below net cash (5.27).
challenges.answer: Rebuilt the terminal year as a steady state: capex equals D&A at 9% of sales and EBIT is positive at 0.54 in FY2035, with FCFF 0.42. The DCF now gives EV 0.75 and equity value Rp1.62/share; terminal value is 266% of EV because the early FCFF is negative, not because the asset is being run down. Both the steady DCF and the book cross-check remain far below Rp224. [S3]

challenges.challenge: The report says the sensitivity table varies the two things that actually decide the answer. The model grid does not: the 12-month value is flat at 16.55 for a 4pp and a 2pp revenue-growth cut (degenerate at the bear), and the whole +/-4pp growth and +/-2pp gross-margin grid spans only 16.55-20.86. The answer is insensitive to the stated key drivers because 94% of value is book-based.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the paragraph to the model actual: the sensitivity is a step, not a slope. The DCF floors at zero once the margin is below the cash-cost level, so the first two gross-margin rows are flat at the asset value; above it a 2pp margin move shifts the target by a few rupiah. Explained that the asset leg governs the answer, so the grid cannot respond like an earnings multiple. [S3, S4]

challenges.challenge: The model contains no shrimp price and no volume; revenue is a single growth rate to Rp59.8bn (2.8x FY2025) on a pond base the report calls fixed, with capex at 6% of sales. That requires revenue per pond of Rp0.98bn by FY2030 against Rp0.45bn in FY2025 and a best-ever Rp0.60bn in FY2023 (48 ponds vs 14), and it is never reconciled to F34 19.07 t/ha benchmark or the 41,966 m2 disclosed.
challenges.answer: Added an explicit revenue-per-pond reconciliation and the disclosure limits. FY2023 revenue per pond spread over 48 ponds lands close to FY2026 revenue, so FY2026 is the full-year run-rate; the FY2030 step needs revenue per pond to rise by more than half again. No tonnage sold and no new-site area are disclosed, so a Rp/kg and t/ha path cannot be sourced; the report states that gap rather than inventing one, and the DCF carries the valuation, not the growth path. [S3, S4]

challenges.challenge: FY+1 does not reproduce the last actual: the engine calibration gate gives FY2026E EBITDA margin 0.29% against 2.02% in FY2025A (gap -1.74pp, about Rp0.5bn, six times FY2026E EBITDA) and nothing in qc_justifications or the text answers it. Separately, a.gross_margin runs -2.0% to +7.0% while the model produces -3.7% to +3.8%, so the drift.gross_margin justification defends a path the model never reaches.
challenges.answer: Reconciled the gap in the justification and the text. FY2026 gross margin is set at base input costs (-2.0%); the soymeal link carries the reviewed deck above its FY2025 average and drags the reported line to -3.7%, so EBITDA margin is 0.29% instead of 2.02%. At FY2025 soymeal the line reproduces 2.02%. Updated drift.gross_margin to defend the -3.7% to +7.4% line the model actually reaches. [S3, S4]

challenges.challenge: The report asserts a buyer would need a margin the company has never reported, but the model own FY2023A line shows revenue Rp8.35bn, gross profit Rp2.56bn (+30.7%) and EBIT +0.23bn. FY2023 is absent from every section. It is the one year on record where the pond model earned a gross margin, and it is the natural bull anchor.
challenges.answer: Added FY2023 audited revenue 8.35, gross profit 2.56 (30.6%), EBIT 0.23 and explained why the pre-expansion economics cannot simply return: the 34 new ponds carry the depreciation that lifted the group charge to 4.48 (F11/F12), and revenue per pond has fallen since FY2023. Even a bull case recovering the full FY2023 margin values the shares far below Rp224. [S11, S3]

challenges.challenge: Revenue fell 62% in FY2024 (Rp8.35bn to Rp3.13bn) with a -66.7% gross margin, a year before the Cesium-137 finding the report blames for the loss; that precedent is never used and the bear case carries neither a harvest-failure shock nor the dilution the narrative promises (shocks are only revenue growth -10pp and gross margin -2pp). Bear lands at 16.55 against base 17.45, so the stated downside is worth -5%.
challenges.answer: Anchored the bear on FY2024 (revenue -62.5%, gross margin -66.9%) and replaced the old two shocks with four mirrored ones: growth -10pp, margin -3pp, G&A +2pp, capex +1pp; the bull mirrors all four. The narrative carries a dilutive placement and the text says the engine does not apply share_change to per-share value, so the bear is an upper bound on dilution, not a model of it. [S3]

challenges.challenge: The base case is not fundable as built: cash is negative from FY2033 (-0.27) to FY2035 (-1.82), debt is capped at Rp2.62bn and net_borrowing is 0.000, while the report itself says the base case needs a working-capital facility. Funding is only in the bear case. The roll-forward also compounds a 94% book-based value at the cost of equity while the forecast erodes book by about 10% a year, and P/B credits Rp10.5bn of title-in-process land advances at 90 cents.
challenges.answer: Added an explicit base-case facility: 0.8 in FY2026, 1.2 in FY2027, 1.6 in FY2028, 1.3 in FY2029, repaid after, with interest. Debt peaks at 5.5 and cash stays positive every year, so the base is funded. Also stated that the engine rolls the blended value at COE while book is falling (29.6 to 26.9 per share), so the correct asset-leg roll is negative and the target is overstated rather than understated. [S3, S4]

challenges.challenge: The valuation uses a 30 June 2026 balance sheet (market block: cash 5.794, debt 0.524, book 48.191, net cash 5.27) that appears in no fact and no archived source, while the text states FY2025 figures (net debt -2.1, tangible book 29.6 per share). With the stated -2.1 the DCF equity is Rp0.2 per share, not the Rp2 printed. The +0.98 FY2026 FCFF also depends entirely on a Rp3.70bn working-capital release (nwc +2.58 FY2025A to -1.12 FY2026E) sourced only to that same vendor snapshot; without it FY2026 FCFF is -2.73.
challenges.answer: Replaced the unsourced June 2026 balance sheet with audited 31 Dec 2025 facts: cash 2.70, debt 0.62, equity 51.80 (F39-F42), and disclosed the valuation date in the text. No archived half-year report exists (the IR page lists only audited annual LK), so the June vendor snapshot is not used. Working capital is held at the audited absolute 2.58bn, removing the Rp3.7bn release; FY2026 FCFF is -2.73, not +0.98. [S2, S3]

challenges.challenge: The scenario block is not reproducible from the model. The text gives bear 0.2, base 0.5, bull 0.2 (sums to 0.9) at Rp15/Rp16/Rp21, which weights to Rp17.0, not the Rp19 target; the model has 0.25/0.5/0.25 at target prices 16.55/17.45/23.19, which weights to 18.66. The 17 June expose did target 2026 acceleration through higher sales volume, cost efficiency and asset optimisation (S5); the text now says so and notes there was no numeric target. [S5, S6, S7]

The company own explanation of the 2026 sell-off, an MSCI index rebalancing (S5), is never mentioned even though an index deletion is the one identifiable forced-selling mechanism.
challenges.answer: Named a mechanism consistent with the data: free float is 49% and ADTV is about 1% of market cap, so this is not scarcity of paper; the company attributes the 2026 sell-off to an MSCI index rebalancing plus Middle East geopolitics. challenges.answer: Market cap now resolves through the |idrb format, printing IDR392bn instead of IDR392,008,976,128.0bn. Lease cost: the report now cites the filing single-digit lease rate (F23 on F21) and explains that the engine prices debt off sovereign plus corporate spread; at a debt weight of 0.16% the WACC effect is a few basis points, not a valuation driver. findings.finding: Section 4 builds the target and does not reproduce it. The paragraph rolls the Rp17 blend forward at 11.9% (16.63 x 1.1186 = 18.61, its own adds Rp19 less Rp17) and then prints the twelve-month target as Rp22. Rp22 is the 30/50/20 probability-weighted scenario average (0.5x18.61 + 0.3x14.82 + 0.2x39.94 = 21.74), which only section 5 explains. This is Q5-class prose arithmetic, not a model error, but it is the headline number stated derivation and a regression introduced when the target moved from Rp19 to Rp22.

The terminal-margin basis and drift.gross_margin justification misdescribe the model. The soymeal link is charged in every forecast year including the terminal (FY2035 COGS drag 4.74pp = 0.12 x 0.80 x (506.40/321.15 - 1) x COGS/revenue), so nothing is released in the terminal state; what changed is the gross-margin path itself (lt 0.07 to 0.144). About 40% above the FY2025 average matches the FY2028-29 deck plateau (449.67/321.15 = +40.0%) but not the FY2035 level (+57.7%), so the justification understates the terminal drag. The level is defensible against the FY2023 30.6% anchor, but the mechanism as written is circular (without that release the perpetuity is negative) and the report text never states the terminal steady-state margin.

The explicit terminal path is still not flat. FCFF falls 1.975 (FY2030) to 1.474 (FY2035), -26%, and EBIT margin 4.15% to 3.16%, because the deck soymeal rises about 2% a year while pass-through is 20%. The Gordon then applies +4%, which is only consistent if the deck stops rising after FY2035, a construction the model does not show. Section 4 settles just below that level understates a quarter decline.

Unit duplication from placeholder-plus-literal strings, 14.0 ponds production ponds and 34.0 ponds ponds in section 1 and 15.0 people permanent staff in section 6. Cosmetic, but it is the kind of thing the formatter sweep should have caught while it was in the file.

The base case draws Rp0.8, 1.8, 1.6 and 1.3bn of facility to FY2029 while cash is already Rp1.5-4.0bn (FY2028 debt 4.82 with cash 1.54; FY2029 debt 6.12 with cash 3.97), paying 8% on debt and earning 2% on cash. Conservative by a few tenths of a rupiah a share and immaterial, but the draw schedule was not re-sized after the gross-margin path was raised.
